Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

The narrative unfolds primarily as a vivid, real-time scene on the ferry, complete with sensory details (the smell of oil and wet wood, the sound of suitcase wheels), physical actions (trying to crank the engine), and sparse, tense dialogue between Ilse and Jonas. Woven seamlessly into this present action are brief moments of exposition and summary—such as the history of the Deutz engine from thirty years ago, the memory of driving Jonas to the train station in Lüneburg when he was seventeen, and the practical details of the ferry and bus schedules. This balance grounds the reader in the immediate moment while efficiently providing just enough backstory to understand the unspoken history and tension between the two characters.
